planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this critically endangered Guangdong native is prized for flowering nearly year-round rather than only in winter like most camellias.

directions: Discovered in the 1980s in a single nature reserve near Yangchun, Guangdong, this species is now critically endangered in the wild but preserved through cultivation and breeding programs worldwide. Unlike almost every other camellia, it produces bright red to salmon blooms in flushes across much of the year, with its heaviest flush in summer, rather than confining its display to the cooler months. This unusual year-round blooming trait has made it a key parent in modern breeding efforts aimed at extending the camellia flowering season. Grow it in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade with reliable moisture, and protect it from hard freezes since it is less cold-hardy than japonica or sasanqua types.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; small glossy leaves and dainty flowers give this species a finer texture than most garden camellias.

directions: Native to south-central China and now rare to possibly extinct in its original wild habitat, this species survives chiefly through cultivated stock held by specialty growers and collectors. It carries small, slightly fragrant, soft pink single to semi-double flowers with contrasting yellow anthers from late winter into early spring, set against finely textured, glossy small leaves on a twiggy, graceful shrub. Its fine-scaled foliage and flowers make it a favorite for bonsai training as well as woodland borders. Grow in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade or filtered sun, avoiding alkaline soil and standing water.

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in sun to partial shade; this large-growing wild relative of the tea plant is native to the Dali region of western Yunnan.

directions: Native to the mountains around Dali in western Yunnan and adjacent northern Myanmar, this species is a close wild relative of the cultivated tea plant and forms the basis of ancient wild tea tree stands still harvested today for highly prized raw pu'er tea. It grows as a large shrub or small tree with bigger leaves than Camellia sinensis, and its creamy white flowers open with a notably higher petal count, giving them a distinctive fried-egg appearance. Give it average, humus-rich, well-drained, acidic soil and a sunny to partially shaded site, since it tolerates more sun than most ornamental camellia species once established. It is less cold-hardy than Chinese-type tea plants, so it fits best in milder zones with protection from hard freezes.
